analysis.one_liner: Suspends faster meat- and poultry-slaughter line speeds during the COVID-19 emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a committee vote or floor action before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the pandemic, the Agriculture Department had allowed some meat and poultry plants to run slaughter lines faster and to convert to a new swine inspection system with no line-speed cap. This bill would have suspended those waivers and blocked any new increases in line speeds until 90 days after the COVID-19 emergency ends, and required the Government Accountability Office and three Cabinet departments to report on how well worker, animal, and food safety was protected during the pandemic.
analysis.who_benefits: Meatpacking and poultry workers — a workforce that is heavily low-wage and immigrant — who face high injury rates and were hit hard by COVID-19 outbreaks in plants. Food Safety and Inspection Service inspectors and consumers would also benefit from slower lines giving inspectors more time to spot contaminated or diseased carcasses, and the bill directs a government review of pandemic protections for workers and animals in these plants [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill suspends existing USDA waivers that let meat and poultry plants run slaughter lines faster than the standard limit, and bars new waivers for line speeds and reduced inspection staffing through 90 days after the COVID-19 emergency is lifted [S2] [S3].
It also suspends implementation of the New Swine Slaughter Inspection System, the 2019 rule that let pork plants speed up lines and shift more inspection duties to company employees [S2] [S3].
It prohibits any USDA funds from being used during the emergency period to develop or implement any policy that would increase line speeds at covered plants [S2] [S3].

It requires a Government Accountability Office review — covering social distancing on production lines, protective equipment, plant outbreaks, humane handling enforcement, and the effect of faster lines on worker protections — and reports from the Agriculture, Labor, and Health and Human Services secretaries within 180 days [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large meat and poultry processors, whose slaughter throughput would drop while the waivers are suspended, raising their per-animal processing costs; some of that cost could be passed to consumers as somewhat higher meat prices. The Agriculture Department would also lose flexibility to modernize its inspection systems during the covered period [S3].

drawbacks.text: Slower line speeds mean fewer animals processed per hour, which raises processing costs and could modestly raise retail meat prices for consumers during the covered period [S3].

The bill is written as a temporary emergency measure, but the funding restriction barring any line-speed increase applies for the entire covered period with no industry or plant-specific flexibility, which critics would call a blunt instrument for an industry employing hundreds of thousands of workers [S3].

USDA's position in the 2019 swine rule was that plant employees could perform some inspection tasks safely under agency oversight; suspending the system entirely rolls back that modernization rather than fixing it [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers and food safety, the bill targeted a specific, documented pandemic-era risk: plants running faster with workers who could not distance, at facilities that became major COVID-19 outbreak sites. The main cost falls on processor throughput and possibly on meat prices, which is a real but modest consumer cost. The design is straightforward rather than elegant — a blanket suspension plus a funding ban — but its scope is explicitly temporary and it preserves stricter state worker-safety and animal-welfare laws.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on March 11, 2021, and the committee never acted on it; it died there when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on March 11, 2021, with 12 original cosponsors — 11 Democrats and one Independent — and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day [S1] [S4] [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the bill received no committee markup, no hearing, no floor vote, and no House companion action recorded in its history before the Congress ended [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meat and poultry processors are better off, because the faster line speeds and the New Swine Slaughter Inspection System the bill would have suspended remain in place, and no GAO review or Cabinet reporting on pandemic-era worker protections was required.

for.name: Cory Booker
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to suspend increased line speeds at meat and poultry plants during the COVID-19 emergency.

for.name: 11 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: 1 of 2 Senate Independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Debbie Stabenow
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Her committee, to which the bill was referred, never scheduled a markup or vote on it during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Meat and poultry processing industry
against.role: Large meatpackers and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on line speeds, which the industry defended as necessary to plant efficiency and as safe under USDA inspection rules; the bill died in committee without any recorded vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 supporters were Democrats or the Independent Senator Sanders; no Republican cosponsored, and the Democratic-controlled Agriculture Committee never acted on the bill [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have suspended their waivers to run slaughter lines faster and halted the swine inspection system, cutting throughput and raising per-unit costs. Because the bill died in committee, the faster line speeds stayed in place — the outcome that serves the industry's interest.

industries.industry: USDA meat and poultry inspection system
industries.note: The bill would have preserved standard inspection staffing and given federal inspectors more time per carcass, but it also froze the department's inspection modernization program during the covered period.
